title: Shreyas Doshi on Product Strategy, Pre-mortems, and the LNO Framework
speaker: Shreyas Doshi
description: Former Stripe, Twitter, and Google product leader Shreyas Doshi discusses product strategy, high-leverage decision making, the LNO task framework, pre-mortems, and opportunity cost thinking.
content:
Lenny Rachitsky: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast. Today my guest is Shreyas Doshi, former product leader at Stripe, Twitter, Google, and Yahoo. Shreyas, thank you so much for joining me today.

Shreyas Doshi: Thanks Lenny, it is great to be here with you.

Lenny Rachitsky: I want to start by asking you about task prioritization. So many product managers and founders are overwhelmed by endless to-do lists. How should they think about allocating their time?

Shreyas Doshi: At a certain point in your career, the scope of your role becomes an immovable force. If you treat every task with equal importance, you will burn out. That is why I created the LNO Framework: Leverage, Neutral, and Overhead.

Lenny Rachitsky: Can you break down how the LNO framework works?

Shreyas Doshi: Absolutely. L stands for Leverage tasks. These are high-impact activities where 1x effort yields a 10x return or outcome. Examples include shaping core product strategy, setting team culture, and writing key architecture specs. On Leverage tasks, you must be a perfectionist and demand exceptional quality.

N stands for Neutral tasks. Here, 1x effort yields 1x outcome. These are standard operational responsibilities—routine status updates, basic review meetings. Do a solid, good job, but do not obsess over perfection.

O stands for Overhead tasks. These are low-impact tasks where 1x effort gives only 0.1x value—filling out compliance forms, routine admin work. On Overhead tasks, your goal is to minimize time: delegate, automate, or intentionally do a passably mediocre job.

Lenny Rachitsky: That concept of strategic neglect is so powerful. What about decision-making before launching major features?

Shreyas Doshi: One of the most effective tools I use is the Pre-mortem. Before launching a major product or initiative, gather the team and ask: 'Imagine we are two years in the future, and this launch was a complete disaster. What went wrong?' By conducting a pre-mortem, team members feel safe highlighting hidden risks, blind spots, and flawed assumptions before writing a single line of code.

Lenny Rachitsky: How does ROI thinking differ from opportunity cost thinking in product leadership?

Shreyas Doshi: Most average product managers think in terms of ROI—'Is this feature worth doing?' Great product leaders think in opportunity cost—'If we spend 3 months building feature A, what high-leverage work on feature B are we giving up?' Strategic focus is about saying no to good ideas so you have bandwidth for game-changing ones.
